node_outputs.N8:
Likely alternative diagnoses and how they fit the presentation

The clinical picture of leg swelling plus a calf difference is broad, but the evidence points to two main competing explanations: deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and lymphoedema. The most directly relevant source says the two main causes of a swollen lower limb are DVT and lymphoedema [N2-R1]. That is a strong starting point for alternative diagnoses, but the evidence also shows that the presence of other features can shift the differential.

A calf difference is a classic DVT sign, not a sign of lymphoedema. The MDCalc Wells criteria explicitly include calf swelling >3 cm compared to the other leg as a positive item, and the excerpt emphasizes that calf swelling of 10 cm below tibial tuberosity is the standard measurement [N2-R2][N2-R4]. The same source also notes that “entire leg swollen” indicates extensive venous obstruction, which supports the idea that a large calf difference can be part of a more-extensive venous blockage rather than just a localized problem [N2-R2]. However, the Cleveland Clinic notes that DVT symptoms include swelling, pain, redness, and warmth, while the Mayo Clinic adds leg pain, cramping, or soreness that often starts in the calf [N3-R1][N3-R4]. So the presence of a calf difference is more consistent with venous obstruction than with the superficial-vein-only picture the patient may be trying to rule out.

Pitting edema is another important feature. The Merck Manuals entry says pitting edema is greater in the affected leg in DVT, and the MDCalc Wells criteria include pitting edema confined to the symptomatic leg as a positive item [N6-R3][N2-R3].
